payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.

17. The heading “Insurance of Motor Vehicles against Third Party Risks” given in Chapter XI of the
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Chapter VIII of 1939 Act) itself shows the intention of the legislature to
make third party insurance compulsory and to ensure that the victims of accident arising out of use
of motor vehicles would be able to get compensation for the death or injuries suffered. The provision
has been inserted in order to protect the persons travelling in vehicles or using the road from the
risk attendant upon the user of the motor vehicles on the road. To overcome this ugly situation, the
legislature has made it obligatory that no motor vehicle shall be used unless a third party insurance

18. Reading the provisions of Sections 146 and 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act, it is evidently clear
that in certain circumstances the insurer’s right is safeguarded but in any event the insurer has to
pay compensation when a valid certificate of insurance is issued notwithstanding the fact that the
insurer may proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount. Under Section 149 of the Motor
Vehicles Act, the insurer can defend the action inter alia on the grounds, namely, (i) the vehicle was
not driven by a named person, (ii) it was being driven by a person who was not having a duly
granted licence, and (iii) person driving the vehicle was disqualified to hold and obtain a driving

args.question: Precedents dealing with fake, forged, expired or otherwise invalid driving licences and their effect on insurance liability

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The Swaran Singh 'pay and recover' principle applies ONLY to third-party claims, not to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, subsequent renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly addresses fake/forged driving licences and distinguishes between third-party and own-damage claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the leading Supreme Court authority on the critical distinction: for third-party claims, the insurer must pay and can recover; for own-damage claims, a fake licence is a complete defence.
supporting.quote: 1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. 2. Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. 3. In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory under Section 149, regardless of breach of policy conditions (including invalid driving licence). The insurer must pay and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that even a conscious, proven breach of licence conditions does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties. The breach must be 'conscious and wilful' but even then, pay-and-recover applies.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: Mere expiry/non-renewal of a driving licence on the accident date does not constitute a 'fundamental breach' absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer remains liable.
supporting.fact_alignment: Drivers' licences had expired before the accident dates and were renewed later. The court held the insurer jointly and severally liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that an expired licence (as opposed to a fake one) is a lesser breach. The driver had held a valid licence earlier; mere non-renewal is not a fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: Mere fact that the driver of the offending vehicle had not got his driving licence renewed on the date of the accident and got it renewed subsequently would not amount to breach of condition of the policy.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had no driving licence at all on the date of accident. The tribunal found a fundamental breach but applied pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that even the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration, for third-party claims.
supporting.quote: It is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver had no valid licence during the interregnum, but the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Licence expired 30.04.2008; accident on 02.07.2008; renewed on 04.07.2008 (beyond 30 days). The court held no valid licence on accident date but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Clarifies the operation of Section 15 of the MV Act on renewal timelines and confirms that even a lapsed licence leads to pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: The insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot avoid third-party liability merely because the driver, holding a valid LMV licence, lacked an endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver held a valid LMV licence but no endorsement to drive a Mahindra Maxi Cab (commercial vehicle). Supreme Court held insurer liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Critical for cases where the licence is valid for the class but lacks a specific endorsement — this is NOT a valid defence against third-party claims.
supporting.quote: The insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Full Bench: Even if a fundamental breach under Section 149(2) is proved, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured. This applies to both Act policies and contractual policies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Comprehensive Full Bench analysis of the insurer's liability despite breach of licence conditions.
supporting.why_it_matters: The most comprehensive ratio on this point — confirms that pay-and-recover is the rule, not the exception, for third-party claims regardless of the type of policy.
supporting.quote: The insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: Where the driver had an LMV licence with a transport endorsement but lacked the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle, the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV + transport endorsement but drove a heavy goods vehicle. The court applied Swaran Singh and ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the principle to cases where the driver had some licence but not the correct class — still pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: In case of Third Party risks the Insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a transport vehicle driver holds only an LMV licence without the required badge/authorisation, there is a breach, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had only LMV licence, no badge to drive a transport vehicle (Maxi Cab). Insurer ordered to pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that missing badge/authorisation for transport vehicles is a breach but does not defeat third-party claims.
supporting.quote: The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Absence of a special endorsement for driving hazardous goods (tanker) constitutes a breach, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had valid licence for MC, LMV, HGV, HTV but no special endorsement for driving a tanker carrying hazardous goods.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the principle to specialised licence requirements under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules — even regulatory breaches lead to pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: For own-damage claims (non-third-party), a fake driving licence is a complete defence — the insurer has no liability at all. Swaran Singh does not apply.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the claim is for own-damage (e.g., damage to the insured vehicle itself, not third-party injury/death), the insurer will cite this to deny all liability. The client cannot rely on pay-and-recover for own-damage claims.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims. If the client's case involves third-party injury/death (which most motor accident claims do), this case actually supports the client — it confirms that for third-party claims, pay-and-recover applies. The key is to establish that the claim is a third-party claim.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks. ... Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without any valid licence is a 'fundamental and statutory breach' of the insurance policy. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that the breach is so fundamental that no liability should attach at all. The tribunal here did find a fundamental breach.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Despite finding a fundamental breach, the tribunal still ordered pay-and-recover in favour of the third-party claimant. The breach only affects the insurer's liability to the owner, not to the third party. The ratio is that even 'no licence' cases result in pay-and-recover for third-party claims.
adverse.quote: It is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability. ... But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
adverse.principle: Where a licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect only from the renewal date, not retrospectively. The driver had no valid licence on the accident date.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that the driver was unlicensed on the accident date because the renewal was delayed beyond 30 days, and Section 15 of the MV Act does not allow retrospective renewal in such cases.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover. The finding that the driver had no valid licence only meant the insurer could recover from the owner — it did not absolve the insurer of liability to the third party. The client can rely on the pay-and-recover order.
adverse.quote: The insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation by 50%.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the claimant/victim himself was driving without a licence, the insurer will argue contributory negligence and seek to reduce the award by 50% or more.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involved the claimant himself driving without a licence and without a helmet — the contributory negligence was based on the totality of conduct, not just the licence issue. Where the victim is a pedestrian or pillion rider, this case is distinguishable. Also, the case is a Tribunal decision, not binding precedent.
adverse.quote: He did not have DL at the time of accident and they all three were not wearing the helmets. Keeping in view of circumstances of the case, the 50% of the total compensation amount is deducted towards contributory negligence.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Pay-and-recover is not available where the claimant was a passenger in a private vehicle being used for hire — such a person is not a 'third party' under the Act.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the victim was travelling in a private vehicle being used for hire/reward (contrary to policy conditions), the insurer may argue that the victim is not a third party and no pay-and-recover applies.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case turns on the specific factual finding that the vehicle was a private vehicle used for hire, which is a different breach (permitted use) from licence invalidity. In standard third-party claims where the victim is a pedestrian or other road user, this case is distinguishable.

adverse.title: D a d a p e e r a S / O A b d u l S a l a m S a b v s M a l l e s h M S / O Hanumanthappa
adverse.principle: Where the victim was travelling on a tractor mud-guard (in violation of vehicle rules), the insurer is not liable and no pay-and-recover order was passed.
adverse.risk_to_client: If the victim was an unauthorised passenger or travelling in a prohibited manner, the insurer may argue that no pay-and-recover applies because the victim is not a 'third party' entitled to statutory protection.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case involves a gratuitous passenger on a tractor mud-guard — a specific exclusion. It does not apply to standard road accident victims (pedestrians, other vehicle occupants) where the only breach is the driver's licence invalidity.

priority_arguments: Lead with the fundamental principle: under Section 149 of the MV Act, the insurer's liability to third parties is STATUTORY, not contractual. Even proven breach of licence conditions results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration (doc_025, doc_033).

Cite Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) to distinguish: for third-party claims (which most motor accident claims are), Swaran Singh applies and pay-and-recover is the rule. The insurer's attempt to avoid liability entirely only works for own-damage claims.
For expired licences: cite K.G. Srinivasamurthy (doc_034) for the proposition that mere non-renewal on the accident date is NOT a fundamental breach — the insurer remains liable.
For missing endorsements/badges: cite S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and Chennamma (doc_027) — the insurer cannot avoid liability for lack of a specific endorsement on an otherwise valid licence.
For no licence at all: cite Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) — even a fundamental breach leads to pay-and-recover for third-party claims.
For delayed renewal beyond 30 days: cite Parvathi Hebbar (doc_003) — the insurer must still pay and recover.

For fake/forged licences: the key distinction from Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) is that a fake licence is a complete defence only for own-damage claims; for third-party claims, pay-and-recover applies.
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — this is a liability/defence research brief, not a quantum assessment.
risks: Own-damage claims: If the client's case involves damage to the insured vehicle (not third-party injury/death), Laxmi Narain Dhut (doc_031) is a HIGH risk — a fake licence is a complete defence and pay-and-recover does not apply.

Contributory negligence: If the victim was driving without a licence, the insurer may argue contributory negligence to reduce the award (doc_009). This is a medium risk that depends on the victim's role in the accident.
Fraud/collusion: If the third party was in collusion with the insured, doc_025 (Yallavva) notes that pay-and-recover may not apply. This is a low-probability but high-impact risk.

Non-third-party victims: If the victim was an unauthorised passenger (e.g., on a tractor mud-guard, or in a private vehicle used for hire), the insurer may argue the victim is not a 'third party' and no pay-and-recover applies (doc_028, doc_030).
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal under Section 166 MV Act. The primary relief sought should be a declaration that the insurer is liable to satisfy the award, with liberty to recover from the owner if breach is proved.

caveats: This corpus does not contain the full text of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 itself, which is the foundational authority on this topic. All the judgments in this corpus cite and apply Swaran Singh. If deeper analysis of Swaran Singh's specific ratio is needed, the original judgment should be consulted separately.

The corpus contains judgments from multiple jurisdictions (Supreme Court, various High Courts, and Tribunals). Tribunal decisions (doc_009, doc_024, doc_034) are persuasive but not binding precedent. Supreme Court decisions (doc_031, doc_032) and Full Bench decisions (doc_025) carry the greatest weight.
This research addresses liability/defence only, not quantum of compensation. Separate quantum analysis would be needed for any specific claim.
The corpus does not contain any judgment dealing specifically with a learner's licence scenario, which was one of the categories identified in Swaran Singh.

payload.holding: The insurance company is not statutorily liable to cover passengers travelling in a goods vehicle, but considering the prolonged litigation and status of the claimants, a 'pay and recover' order is issued against the insurance company.
payload.ratio: The insurance company has no statutory liability to pay compensation to passengers travelling in a goods vehicle, but appellate courts retain the discretion to apply the 'pay and recover' doctrine depending on the facts and circumstances of each case.

args.question: Precedents dealing with fake, forged, expired or otherwise invalid driving licences and their effect on insurance liability

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The Swaran Singh 'pay and recover' principle applies ONLY to third-party claims, not to own-damage claims. Where the licence was originally fake, subsequent renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly addresses fake/forged driving licences and distinguishes between third-party and own-damage claims.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the leading Supreme Court authority on the critical distinction: for third-party claims, the insurer must pay and can recover; for own-damage claims, a fake licence is a complete defence.
supporting.quote: 1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. 2. Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. 3. In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory under Section 149, regardless of breach of policy conditions (including invalid driving licence). The insurer must pay and may recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver possessed only an LMV (non-transport) licence but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial). The court held the insurer liable to third parties with recovery rights.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that even a conscious, proven breach of licence conditions does not absolve the insurer vis-à-vis third parties. The breach must be 'conscious and wilful' but even then, pay-and-recover applies.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: Mere expiry/non-renewal of a driving licence on the accident date does not constitute a 'fundamental breach' absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The insurer remains liable.
supporting.fact_alignment: Drivers' licences had expired before the accident dates and were renewed later. The court held the insurer jointly and severally liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Establishes that an expired licence (as opposed to a fake one) is a lesser breach. The driver had held a valid licence earlier; mere non-renewal is not a fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: Mere fact that the driver of the offending vehicle had not got his driving licence renewed on the date of the accident and got it renewed subsequently would not amount to breach of condition of the policy.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without any valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must still pay the third-party claimant and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had no driving licence at all on the date of accident. The tribunal found a fundamental breach but applied pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Shows that even the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration, for third-party claims.
supporting.quote: It is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1, owner of the offending vehicle.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal, not retrospectively. The driver had no valid licence during the interregnum, but the insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: Licence expired 30.04.2008; accident on 02.07.2008; renewed on 04.07.2008 (beyond 30 days). The court held no valid licence on accident date but ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Clarifies the operation of Section 15 of the MV Act on renewal timelines and confirms that even a lapsed licence leads to pay-and-recover, not exoneration.
supporting.quote: The insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot avoid third-party liability merely because the driver, holding a valid LMV licence, lacked an endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver held a valid LMV licence but no endorsement to drive a Mahindra Maxi Cab (commercial vehicle). Supreme Court held insurer liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: Critical for cases where the licence is valid for the class but lacks a specific endorsement — this is NOT a valid defence against third-party claims.
supporting.quote: The insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Full Bench: Even if a fundamental breach under Section 149(2) is proved, the insurer must satisfy the third-party award and recover from the insured. This applies to both Act policies and contractual policies.
supporting.fact_alignment: Comprehensive Full Bench analysis of the insurer's liability despite breach of licence conditions.
supporting.why_it_matters: The most comprehensive ratio on this point — confirms that pay-and-recover is the rule, not the exception, for third-party claims regardless of the type of policy.
supporting.quote: The insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: Where the driver had an LMV licence with a transport endorsement but lacked the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle, the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had LMV + transport endorsement but drove a heavy goods vehicle. The court applied Swaran Singh and ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Extends the principle to cases where the driver had some licence but not the correct class — still pay-and-recover.
supporting.quote: In case of Third Party risks the Insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where a transport vehicle driver holds only an LMV licence without the required badge/authorisation, there is a breach, but the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured.
